abstract: Rapid training of terrain-aware locomotion requires both high simulation throughput and trajectories that remain informative for learning. We combine Isaac Gym simulation, observation and reward computation, and proximal policy optimization on one GPU, reducing CPU-GPU data transfers. A performance-adaptive curriculum moves robots among prebuilt terrain tiles, increasing difficulty after successful traversal and reducing it when progress is insufficient. This supplies progressively challenging experience without regenerating terrain, while one policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights to follow motion commands. With 4,096 robots, batches of 98,304 samples, and 1,500 policy updates, an ANYmal C policy trains in under 20 minutes on an RTX A6000 workstation. Parallelism remains constrained by the need for adequate consecutive rollout steps per robot; shorter trajectories can undermine learning. Simulation tests show nearly complete traversal success on stairs up to 0.2 m, but declining success on randomized obstacles and unsuccessful climbing beyond 25-degree slopes. The fixed policy also negotiates stairs and obstacles on hardware, where imperfect elevation maps reduce robustness and motivate limiting commanded speed to 0.6 m/s. These experiments establish rapid training and physical deployment under the reported configuration, with limits from rollout duration and terrain sensing.
methods: PPO's critic estimates an infinite-horizon discounted return, so a reset must be interpreted according to why it occurs. Failure or goal completion ends the task trajectory, whereas a time limit interrupts an otherwise continuing trajectory. Because episode time is omitted from observations, the critic cannot anticipate the time-out from its input. Assigning zero continuation value at that reset would truncate its target for an unobserved reason. The environment therefore flags time-outs separately and augments their rewards with the critic's discounted prediction of future return, bootstrapping the target instead of treating truncation as terminal. This estimate belongs to the interrupted trajectory, not the new episode after reset. The distinction is essential here because 20-second episodes span many short rollout batches, and environments are not reset after each policy update. Consequently, time-outs can occur within batches; assuming that they never occur or occur only at collection boundaries would miss these cases.
results: Figure 4 identifies a bounded reward-time trade-off, not a monotonic benefit of parallelism. On a simplified task with the curriculum removed, it reports mean episode reward and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. Within each fixed batch size, adding robots shortens per-robot rollouts and reduces training time, but excessive parallelism sharply lowers reward. The authors attribute this decline to insufficient temporal information for advantage estimation; their explanation for lower reward at small robot counts is reduced sample diversity, not an isolated causal finding. Throughput scales nearly linearly up to about 4,000 robots, then improves more slowly. Larger batches raise reward and delay the short-rollout deterioration, but require more training time; the million-sample, 20,000-robot baseline gives the highest reward at a longer training duration. Thus, roughly 2,048-4,096 robots with batches near 100,000-200,000 samples offer the reported compromise for this task. That choice balances trajectory length, data diversity, and computational throughput rather than showing that arbitrarily many robots improve learning.
notes: Training time refers to the reported i9-11900k/RTX A6000 workstation configuration, not hardware execution speed. Simulation traversal success requires crossing the terrain without base contact. Figure 4 removes the curriculum and reduces maximum stair and obstacle difficulty; its five-run reward dispersion is not a hardware success estimate. The source does not supply exact plotted rewards, training-time coordinates, or hardware trial counts, so none are inferred. The rollout-length warning is empirical, not a universal threshold. Hardware transfer uses a fixed policy with randomized simulation conditions and an actuator model; imperfect elevation maps remain a deployment limitation.
